turns.text: Hi, Farhan. Can you hear me clearly?
Hi, Daniel. Yes, I can hear you. Is my audio okay?
It is. There was a brief delay when you joined, but it seems stable now. If it changes, we'll pause rather than talk over the connection.
Sounds good. Thank you.

We have about forty-five minutes. We'll spend most of it on a system-design problem. I care about requirements, tradeoffs, and failure behavior more than drawing every possible component. I'll redirect if we need to move on.
Yes, that works for me.
Before we get into the main round, could you give me a brief description of yourself and what you've been working on recently?

I'm a backend and platform engineer whose recent work includes event-driven messaging and preferences services in Kotlin. I have designed event-driven and data-intensive services, operated them on call, and led bounded migrations. I have not built every feature in today's prompt at the exact stated scale, so I will use the requirements we establish rather than pretend my previous architecture transfers unchanged.
What architecture or operational decision in that work was specifically yours?

In my current work on event-driven messaging and preferences services in Kotlin, I owned the service boundary, failure contract, and rollout metrics for one major change. A staff engineer reviewed the design, two engineers shared implementation, and another team owned the upstream producer. My decisions were the consistency boundary, the recovery behavior, and when staged traffic could advance.
Design a notification platform that sends product events through email, mobile push, and SMS.
Who are the users, and which actions are in scope?

Internal teams submit typed notification intents. The platform resolves user preferences and templates, sends through one or more channels, records status, supports scheduled messages, and lets support inspect or retry failures. Marketing campaign authoring is out of scope.
What scale, read-write shape, and latency should drive the design?

Five hundred million channel deliveries per day, normal peak fifty thousand per second, campaign bursts higher, fifty million users, and several thousand internal producer applications. Transactional notifications should begin within ten seconds; bulk messages can be delayed.
Which correctness, availability, or ordering promises matter most?

Do not send a user a channel they opted out of. Transactional traffic must not be starved by bulk campaigns. Delivery is at least once internally, with deduplication keys and provider-specific ambiguity. Preferences may be eventually cached but opt-outs need fast propagation.
Should I include user-interface implementation, billing, and advanced analytics?
No. Define backend APIs and behavior, but exclude UI implementation, billing, and features not named in scope.
May I choose a home region or should every write be active-active globally?
Start with the simplest regional model that meets the requirement. Explain what would force you to add multi-region write complexity.
What retention, audit, and deletion behavior should I preserve?
Retain operational history long enough for customer support and audit. State a reasonable policy and separate reversible soft deletion from irreversible cleanup.

I'll design the core actions and contracts just named, optimize for the stated peak and quality priorities, and exclude the advanced features. I will identify the source of truth, one detailed write and read path, then test failures and regional behavior. The most important domain constraints appear to be: Do not send a user a channel they opted out of. Transactional traffic must not be starved by bulk campaigns. Delivery is at least once internally, with deduplication keys and provider-specific ambiguity. Preferences may be eventually cached but opt-outs need fast propagation.
That scope is right. Go ahead.

At five hundred million deliveries per day, average throughput is about fifty-eight hundred per second but the supplied peak is almost ten times that. Status and attempt records dominate row count, while rendered bodies can be stored separately with short retention. Provider quotas and burst isolation, rather than raw CPU, are likely first-order constraints.
Which assumption in that estimate is weakest, and which decision would change if it is wrong?

The distribution tail is weaker than the average: hot tenants, large payloads, or fan-out can dominate even when aggregate volume looks manageable. I would measure the ninety-fifth and ninety-ninth percentiles and enforce explicit limits. The estimate supports separating high-volume immutable data from control metadata, but I would not purchase capacity or choose a partition count from one median number.
What correctness or product invariants are you protecting?

Do not send a user a channel they opted out of. Transactional traffic must not be starved by bulk campaigns. Delivery is at least once internally, with deduplication keys and provider-specific ambiguity. Preferences may be eventually cached but opt-outs need fast propagation. I would also require idempotent client retries, an auditable state transition for every durable mutation, and bounded recovery so an outage cannot convert into a second overload incident.
Walk me through the high-level design.

A notification API authenticates producers and persists an idempotent intent. An orchestrator resolves audience, preference, template version, locale, and channel plan, then writes channel-delivery records through an outbox. Priority queues feed channel-specific workers. Provider adapters enforce quotas, sign requests, classify responses, and record attempts. Scheduled work uses time buckets; analytics and support views read separate projections.
Where is the source of truth?

The authoritative control and user-visible state follows this model: NotificationIntent stores producer, user or audience reference, event type, template version, variables, priority, schedule, and deduplication key. ChannelDelivery stores user, channel, rendered-body reference, preference version, status, next attempt, and provider message ID. Attempt is append-only. Preference is authoritative by user and channel with version and updated time. Caches, indexes, analytics, and queues are derived or transport layers; each needs a named freshness and rebuild path.
Walk one accepted write through the system.

For a transactional event, persist the intent, resolve current preferences, select template and locale, create channel records, enqueue by priority, and let workers send through adapters. A provider timeout creates an ambiguous result; retry uses a stable client reference where supported and the customer-facing status remains explicit about uncertainty.
Where do you need idempotency?

At the public mutation boundary, at every database-to-queue handoff, and at consumers that can repeat an external effect. I use a caller-scoped idempotency key or stable domain identifier, persist the result with the mutation, and make duplicates return the original outcome. Idempotency does not turn an ambiguous external timeout into exactly once; it only bounds effects we control.
You introduced several components. What would you remove from version one?

Begin with three priority classes, per-provider adapter queues, centralized preference reads with short caches, and a relational control plane. Add fine-grained campaign fairness only after measuring noisy producers.
I heard a technology reflex in that answer. Reconsider it.

Farhan initially suggests one queue per channel, then realizes transactional and bulk isolation also require priority and tenant or producer fairness within each channel. The correction is to restate the required capability first and select the simplest component the team can operate reliably.
How do you partition without creating a hot customer?

Use a high-cardinality stable key for the primary write path and retain tenant as an authorization and fairness dimension. Very large tenants can be promoted to dedicated shards or scheduling buckets. I would not make tenant ID the only physical partition key when the prompt explicitly permits one tenant to dominate traffic.
What changes at ten times scale?

I would first identify the measured bottleneck: edge bandwidth, hot metadata, queue lag, connection count, or background fan-out. Then scale that dimension through more partitions, regional reads, batching, or asynchronous work. I would not add multi-region consensus merely because the traffic number has another zero.
How do you turn the traffic estimate into an initial capacity plan?

I separate steady state, stated peak, and controlled recovery load. Stateless services can begin with enough replicas for roughly twice the normal peak while autoscaling on saturation and queue age, but stateful partitions require measured item size, write amplification, replication, and hot-key headroom. I would load-test the dominant path and set an explicit admission limit before launch. Capacity without a rejection or backpressure policy is only an optimistic chart. For this design, I would verify it specifically at the queues boundary rather than assume the generic rule is enough.
What is your consistency model from the user's perspective?

Authoritative mutations use conditional or transactional writes in the home ownership boundary. Derived caches, indexes, analytics, and regional replicas are eventually consistent with a stated objective. For each stale read I name the user consequence and whether the system may serve stale, fail closed, or bypass the cache. Security revocation and destructive state receive a tighter propagation path than ordinary analytics freshness. For this design, I would verify it specifically at the preferences boundary rather than assume the generic rule is enough.
How do schema changes remain compatible during a rolling deployment?

Use versioned contracts and expand-migrate-contract: add fields or readers first, keep old writers valid, backfill or dual-read with measurable comparison, move writers, then remove the old form only after usage reaches zero. Consumers ignore unknown additive fields where safe. A breaking semantic change receives a new version rather than reusing the same field name with a different meaning. For this design, I would verify it specifically at the fan-out boundary rather than assume the generic rule is enough.
What lifecycle applies to the largest or fastest-growing data?

Classify data by operational need, support window, audit, and legal retention. Hot state stays queryable; immutable payloads or history move to cheaper storage with indexes for bounded retrieval; expired derivatives can be rebuilt or deleted. Deletion is a workflow with tombstone, asynchronous cleanup, verification, and legal-hold checks. I would track bytes by tenant and class so retention policy has a measurable cost. For this design, I would verify it specifically at the retries boundary rather than assume the generic rule is enough.
How do you test correctness beyond unit tests?

Use contract tests at API and event boundaries, deterministic fault injection for timeout and duplicate delivery, replay of representative production shapes with sensitive data removed, and invariant checks on sampled state. Staging should test recovery from partial completion, not only happy-path throughput. Before launch I would run a game day for the failure that creates the most ambiguous external or customer-visible state. For this design, I would verify it specifically at the observability boundary rather than assume the generic rule is enough.
How would you control infrastructure cost without hiding product risk?

Measure cost per successful user outcome, not only per request. The largest levers are retention, replication, egress, fan-out, cache efficiency, and retry amplification. I would set budgets and alert on trend, then change compression, lifecycle, batching, or tiering with correctness guardrails. Removing redundancy or shortening audit retention purely to hit a bill target requires an explicit product and risk decision. For this design, I would verify it specifically at the queues boundary rather than assume the generic rule is enough.
What does a safe migration from an existing system look like?

Inventory callers and data ownership, define compatibility, then use shadow reads or dual calculations where results can be compared. Backfill is partitioned and resumable, with rate limits so it cannot starve normal traffic. Cut over by low-risk tenant or region, retain a bounded rollback path, and stop dual behavior after evidence and a deadline; permanent dual writes create a second source of truth. For this design, I would verify it specifically at the preferences boundary rather than assume the generic rule is enough.
If one partition becomes hot, how do you detect and repair it?

Observe per-partition throughput, latency, queue age, key distribution, and throttling. Short-term mitigation can isolate or rate-limit the hot key, increase cache or consumer capacity, and protect other shards. Durable repair may split by a secondary hash, promote a large tenant, or change a fan-out model. Repartitioning needs a versioned routing map and gradual movement so clients do not guess ownership. For this design, I would verify it specifically at the fan-out boundary rather than assume the generic rule is enough.
What changes if the home region is unavailable for several hours?

Read-only or bounded-stale operations can fail over to a replica if the product accepts the state. For writes, promote only after fencing the old region and confirming the recovery point; otherwise two authorities can diverge. Queue new work durably where possible and expose delayed state. When the region returns, reconcile from versioned logs and drain deliberately instead of replaying every operation at full speed. For this design, I would verify it specifically at the retries boundary rather than assume the generic rule is enough.
How do privacy and data minimization affect observability?

Carry stable opaque identifiers rather than payloads, redact credentials and content at the logging library, limit tenant-level access, and retain detailed traces for a bounded window. Metrics use low-cardinality dimensions; high-cardinality investigation moves to indexed logs with access audit. Sampling must preserve errors and rare security states. Debuggability is a requirement, but collecting every customer field is not the only way to achieve it. For this design, I would verify it specifically at the observability boundary rather than assume the generic rule is enough.
What SLO would you publish, and what happens when it is missed?

Publish the user-visible latency, availability, or freshness objective that matches the core path, plus a correctness indicator that is not hidden by fast failures. Error-budget burn triggers a response proportional to rate and duration: investigate, pause risky rollout, or shift capacity. The SLO should influence prioritization; if misses create only a dashboard color, it is not operating the system. For this design, I would verify it specifically at the queues boundary rather than assume the generic rule is enough.
Give me the minimum useful data model.

NotificationIntent stores producer, user or audience reference, event type, template version, variables, priority, schedule, and deduplication key. ChannelDelivery stores user, channel, rendered-body reference, preference version, status, next attempt, and provider message ID. Attempt is append-only. Preference is authoritative by user and channel with version and updated time.
Which APIs define the product contract?

POST /notifications requires producer ID and idempotency key; GET /notifications/{id} returns aggregate status; POST /deliveries/{id}/retry creates an audited replay. Preference APIs are owned by a separate user service but exposed through a versioned read contract.
How do you prevent a database write followed by a failed queue publish from losing work?

Write an outbox record in the same transaction as the authoritative mutation. A publisher sends it at least once and marks progress. Consumers deduplicate using the stable entity or event ID. If the chosen data store lacks multi-record transactions, co-locate the state and outbox in one atomic item or use a durable log as the source rather than hand-wave a cross-system transaction.
What data belongs outside the primary control store?

Large immutable bytes, append-only raw events, search indexes, and analytics aggregates should use stores suited to those access patterns. The primary control store retains identifiers, ownership, versions, state, and references. Separation reduces cost and hot-row pressure, but each external object needs lifecycle and consistency rules so metadata cannot point forever at missing content.
How are concurrent updates handled?

Use version numbers or conditional writes for user-visible mutable state. A stale client receives a conflict and refreshes rather than overwriting a newer decision. For workflows, state transitions are explicit and monotonic where possible; background workers carry the version or fencing token they claimed.
What would you cache?

Cache only read-heavy values with a clear invalidation or bounded-staleness rule. Include entity version in the cached value, use jittered TTLs, and protect misses with request coalescing. Security revocation and destructive state usually need shorter TTLs or an active invalidation path than ordinary immutable content.
Pressure-test the design against provider outage and failover. What happens and how does it recover?

For provider outage and failover, I first preserve the source-of-truth invariant and prevent unbounded retry. The system records an explicit degraded state, uses deadlines, backoff, jitter, and idempotent transitions, and exposes the condition through user-impact metrics. Recovery is controlled rather than releasing the whole backlog at once. For this design specifically, the affected component follows the ownership boundary already described, and any ambiguous external effect remains visible rather than being relabeled success.

How do you protect healthy tenants while recovering a backlog?

Separate new work from retries, reserve capacity for the normal path, and apply tenant and endpoint admission controls. Recovery drains by oldest age and priority while watching saturation and downstream success. A large failed tenant cannot consume every worker merely because its queue is deepest.
What is the disaster-recovery posture?

Start with replicated durable data and a tested regional failover procedure. If the design uses a home write region, failover requires a fencing or promotion decision before writes resume elsewhere. Read paths may fail over sooner if bounded staleness is acceptable. Define recovery-time and recovery-point objectives rather than claiming instant lossless failover.
Give me the highest-risk security controls.

Authenticate producer applications, authorize event types and templates, encrypt contact data, redact message bodies from ordinary logs, restrict template variables, audit replays and preference changes, and prevent internal producers from sending arbitrary unreviewed content. I would threat-model the public or cross-tenant boundary and make authorization part of the normal data path, not a gateway-only assumption.
What would you alert on?

Time to first attempt by priority, accepted-to-delivered latency, opt-out violations, provider response categories, oldest queue age, deduplication hits, rendered-template failures, and spend or quota saturation by channel. Alerts should connect to user impact or exhaustion trends; dashboards alone are not an operating mechanism.
How does support trace one customer's report?

Expose a safe request, entity, and attempt identifier to the customer. Carry it through logs, queue messages, traces, and state history. Support can retrieve status without viewing sensitive payloads, while operators can pivot by region, shard, response category, and version.
How would you roll out the riskiest change?

Use shadow reads or dual writes only where their comparison semantics are clear, then canary by tenant and region with automated rollback thresholds. Validate recovery, not only success. Keep old readers compatible until the migration checkpoint proves they are no longer needed.
Give me a short recap and name the tradeoff you would expect me to challenge.

The platform persists idempotent intents, resolves preferences and versioned templates, and creates channel-specific delivery obligations through an outbox. Priority and fairness protect transactional traffic; adapters isolate provider semantics; attempts and replays are auditable. The central tradeoff is fast cached preference reads versus opt-out freshness, so invalidation and a conservative send-time recheck for sensitive channels deserve scrutiny.
I have what I need. What questions do you have for me?
Which part of this system is hardest for the team in production today?
Preference correctness and provider ambiguity create more risk than ordinary queue throughput.
That aligns with the failure cases we discussed.
How are design decisions reviewed across time zones?
The author posts a short proposal with a deadline and named decider. Most comments are asynchronous; unresolved tradeoffs get a focused overlap call and a written decision afterward.
That is the working model I'm looking for.
Those were my main questions. Thank you for the context and for your time.
I need to finish my notes and compare them with the rest of the interview team, so I won't give feedback on this call. The recruiter will contact you about the next step within a few business days.
Understood. Thank you, Daniel. Have a good day.
You too, Farhan. Take care.
